Neoclassicism was an eighteenth-century artistic and architectural revival that sought to revive the ideals and forms of classical antiquity—Greece and Rome—as a reaction against the ornate excesses of Baroque and Rococo aesthetics. Driven by Enlightenment ideals of reason, order, and virtue, it emphasized clarity, symmetry, and moral seriousness. The movement profoundly shaped not only visual art but also architecture, literature, and political ideology, particularly in the context of revolution and nation-building.

Neoclassicism emerged in the mid-eighteenth century as a conscious counter-movement to Baroque and Rococo excess and frivolity. It was grounded in Enlightenment philosophy—the belief that reason, clarity, and virtue were the highest ideals worth pursuing. Artists and architects privileged linear clarity, geometric symmetry, and restrained color palettes over the dynamism and ornamentation of preceding styles.

The movement featured subjects drawn from classical mythology and history, chosen for their moral and civic virtue—heroes, republics, duty, sacrifice. It became the official aesthetic of revolutionary governments. The French Revolution adopted it; Neoclassical style dominated Washington, D.C., and American public architecture.

Key practitioners included Jacques-Louis David, whose The Oath of the Horatii became a manifesto for the movement's moral seriousness. The movement extended to architecture and design, where the orders of classical grammar—Doric, Ionic, Corinthian—were restored to dominance in public buildings.

Neoclassicism waned in the mid-nineteenth century as Romanticism reasserted emotion and individualism, though Neoclassical civic architecture continues to dominate governmental institutions worldwide. Its legacy persists in the marble porticoes of courthouses and capitals, still invoking reason and stability through the forms of ancient democracy.
